description: Hey, I'm Pushkar, an IT student from Pune. Going solo for Space Apps this year to build a full-stack web app around NASA's open datasets using Python and JS. Mostly focused on data visualization and clean UI. Excited to see what everyone in the Pune chapter builds!
summary: I built a website that helps you check whether a change in Earth data is real or just random noise. You pick a variable, see its monthly data as a chart with a trend line, and the site tells you the rate of change and whether it is statistically significant. I made it simple enough for students, with plain explanations of every number. I chose this challenge because “is this trend real?” is the question behind most climate headlines, and I wanted anyone to be able to test it themselves.
details:
The site treats Earth data like the brightness of a star over time. Each month is one dot on a chart, and a line shows the overall direction. Then it tests that line in three ways: a t-test with a 95% confidence interval, the Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope, and a shuffle test where the months are scrambled 2,000 times to see how often pure chance gives a slope as steep as the real one. It then gives a one-line verdict.

The first example uses real NASA data: the GISS global temperature record from 1980 to October 2026. It shows a rise of about 0.21 °C per decade, and all three tests agree it is not chance. You can also paste your own NASA table, such as one from Giovanni, and there are sliders to change the time window, noise and trend so you can see how the answer changes. A short finder explains variables from MODIS, OMI, AIRS, GPM, MERRA-2 and GLDAS in simple words.

I wrote it in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the statistics coded in the page itself. It only tests straight-line trends, and monthly data can be linked from one month to the next, which can make results look more certain than they are. I mention this on the site.
